source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments (JDM 11(5))
finding: The training was an under-one-hour online module given to randomly assigned forecasters in four yearly IARPA tournaments. Trained forecasters beat controls on Brier score in all four years.
numbers: Raw mean Brier, control vs trained: Y1 0.42 vs 0.38 (prob, n=119) and 0.38 (scenario, n=113), control n=152, gains 10% and 11%; Y2 0.39 vs 0.34, n=194 vs 205, 12%, t(395)=5.95; Y3 0.34 vs 0.32, n=116 vs 97, 6%, t(207)=2.32, p=.021; Y4 0.38 vs 0.35, 7%, t(225)=2.20, p=.028. Abstract: 6 to 11% over control.
quote: it consistently improved accuracy (Brier scores) by 6 to 11% over the control condition
limits: Gains shrank from Y2 (12%) to Y3 (6%) even as the module grew richer. Y4 text swaps the n and mean labels versus Table 4; Table 4 shows trained as better. Participants were self-selected volunteers who made over 30 forecasts per year.
agent_relevance: A short training module can move probability accuracy by a few percent to about ten percent. Our agent cannot take a module, but its content can be turned into fixed steps in the scaffold.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments (JDM 11(5))
finding: Training content evolved by year but never exceeded one hour. Y1 had two modules: probability training and scenario training. Y2 merged them. Y3 added the S and the KNOW political module and graphics. Y4 was nearly the same with S reworded to level of effort.
numbers: Y1 probability module: coherence under the sum rule, challenge assumptions, base rates, update on evidence, average independent evidence, calibration vs resolution, models, biases. CHAMPS = Comparison classes, Hunt for information, Adjust and update, Mathematical models, Post-mortem, Select questions/effort. KNOW = Know the players, Norms of institutions, Other perspectives, Wildcards. Quizzes added in Y2-Y3.
limits: Training package changed each year, so effects cannot be pinned to one component by design. Authors say which prong helps is untested experimentally.
agent_relevance: This is the exact checklist our scaffold can encode. Each letter maps to an operator: reference class, search, update, model, post-mortem, triage.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments (JDM 11(5))
finding: Among CHAMPS KNOW principles, only the use of comparison classes (outside view, base rates) was clearly tied to better scores in Y4 self-reports. Math/statistical models and question selection also looked good. Post-mortem and Other perspectives looked worse.
numbers: Mean standardized Brier by cited principle (Y4 trained, forecast explanations): Comparison classes 0.17 (n=580); Math/stat models 0.26 (n=453); Select 0.26 (n=330); Hunt 0.38 (n=2,992); Adjust 0.44; Post-mortem 1.04 (n=88); Other perspectives 0.63; all trained categorized 0.42 vs control 0.49. ANOVA: only C, P, O significant. 69% of 6,714 trained explanations were self-classified into a principle; 6,622 control explanations.
limits: Correlational, self-labelled, assumes independence of forecasts. Post-mortem is cited after errors, so it looks bad by selection. Authors warn against concluding only comparison classes matter.
agent_relevance: Supports putting the outside view first in the agent. It also warns that a step used after an error (post-mortem) is not evidence the step hurts.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments (JDM 11(5))
finding: Training effect was partly carried by practice: trained forecasters made more forecasts per question, and that mediated accuracy in three of four years. Experience alone (a past tournament year) did not help; targeted practice did.
numbers: Mediation indirect effect Y1 -0.02, 95% CI -0.04 to -0.01 (p=.01); Y3 -0.02, CI -0.04 to -0.01 (p=.05); Y2 mediation reported significant; Y4 not significant (p=.20, n=221). Trained and control reported similar time: 4.1 vs 3.7 hours/week. Total forecast counts did not differ.
limits: Mediation analysis with an observational mediator, not randomized. Y4 null.
agent_relevance: Training works together with repeated updating and feedback. For a single-pass agent without feedback the training effect may shrink. Build in resolved-question practice only where feedback exists.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments (JDM 11(5))
finding: Cognitive ability and training had mostly independent effects on accuracy. No reliable interaction of training with ability or practice after Y1.
numbers: Some ability measures predicted Brier in all years; numeracy and spatial reasoning did not. Y1 had a significant ability-by-training interaction (most skilled trained did best), not significant in later years. Training had the highest explanatory power among predictors in the individual-difference regressions.
limits: Volunteer sample; ability measures varied by year.
agent_relevance: Training adds on top of raw ability. A stronger base model and a scaffold should be additive, not substitutes.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments (JDM 11(5))
finding: Review of debiasing inside the paper: didactic (information-only) debiasing is cheapest and least effective; process-based and reference-class teaching beat awareness; format changes (frequencies, nested sets) help; feedback helps calibration and resolution.
numbers: Cites Arkes 1991 and Graber 2003 (didactic weak); Case, Fantino & Goodie 1999, Fischhoff & Bar-Hillel 1984, Flyvbjerg 2008, Lovallo, Clarke & Camerer 2012 (reference class beats naming the bias); Gigerenzer & Hoffrage 1995 (frequency formats); Lehman & Nisbett 1990 (r=0.16, p<.06 between SAT and gain from statistics training).
limits: Secondary summary inside the paper, not re-checked against the originals.
agent_relevance: For the agent, a plain warning about overconfidence is the weakest lever. Process steps with a required output are the stronger design.

source: Moore, Swift, Minster, Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Yang, Tenney (2017) Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition (Management Science 63(11))
finding: Training reduced overconfidence in a large field sample, and the reduction held over the whole forecasting year, including months after the module.
numbers: Data: 494,552 forecasts, 344 questions, 2,860 forecasters, three years. Overconfidence (confidence minus hit rate): autonomous no-training 4.3%, autonomous trained 2.0%, team no-training 2.8%, team trained 0.7%. Confidence 64.9 vs 63.5 (autonomous), hit rate 60.7 vs 61.5. Authors say an hour of training halves overconfidence over the following year; abstract: overall overconfidence 3%, 1% with teams plus training.
quote: an hour of training halves overconfidence over the following year
limits: Forecasters also got feedback on scores, which authors say may have cemented the training. Binary and multi-option questions pooled. Effect is a few percentage points of confidence, small in absolute size.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that a one-hour calibration lesson can last a year, but with feedback. Our agent has no memory of feedback across items unless we give it a calibration log.

source: Moore, Swift, Minster, Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Yang, Tenney (2017) Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition (Management Science 63(11))
finding: Training mostly changed calibration by lowering confidence; it improved accuracy only slightly. Teaming mainly improved accuracy. Neither effect interacted with time.
numbers: Table 1 hit rate: 60.7 (none) to 61.5 (trained) autonomous; 62.9 to 63.6 in teams. Confidence fell 1.4 points autonomous and 1.5 in teams.
limits: Effect on accuracy small; calibration gain comes mostly from lower confidence rather than better discrimination.
agent_relevance: Training here is a confidence-shrinking tool. For an LLM that is already overconfident, shrinking toward base rates is a cheap post-step the program could do.

source: Moore, Swift, Minster, Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Yang, Tenney (2017) Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition (Management Science 63(11))
finding: The training had four parts: outside view (how often similar events happened), averaging across opinions, using mathematical and statistical models such as Bayes, and education on biases including overconfidence and excess caution.
numbers: Components cited to Kahneman & Lovallo 1993 (outside view), Larrick & Soll 2006 (averaging). Material on OSF: osf.io/ecmk6.
limits: Components not separated experimentally.
agent_relevance: Same four moves as the scaffold: outside view, average several estimates, model, bias warning. Outside view and averaging can be forced by code.

source: Moore, Swift, Minster, Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Yang, Tenney (2017) Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition (Management Science 63(11))
finding: Earlier calibration training studies gave benefits that decayed and did not generalize. The GJP result is the first with a year of follow-up in the field.
numbers: Lichtenstein & Fischhoff 1980: 45 min training then 22 hour-long test sessions. Stone & Opel 2000: 6 test sessions of 2 hours. Both showed less overconfidence but degradation over time and limited transfer.
limits: As described in Moore et al.; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Training gains can fade without repeated feedback. Each agent call is fresh, so the lesson must be in the prompt every time.

source: Moore, Swift, Minster, Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Yang, Tenney (2017) Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition (Management Science 63(11))
finding: Self-rated expertise did not predict calibration, accuracy or Brier score in the tournament, so people who feel expert are not safer.
numbers: Figure 5: confidence-accuracy curves for expertise levels 1 to 5 were not reliably different.
limits: Self-rating on each question, no external check.
agent_relevance: Do not let the agent's stated familiarity change how much weight it gives its own guess.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament (Psychological Science)
finding: First randomized field test of two training modules in the first two tournament years. Probability training beat scenario training, which beat no training. The benefit lasted across two periods of 8 to 10 months with a module of about 45 minutes.
numbers: Y1: F(2,1586)=14.29, p<.001; probability vs scenario t(1053)=2.23, p=.026; scenario vs none t(1056)=3.25, p<.001. Y2: probability vs none F(1,882)=19.12, p<.001. Y1 began with 2,246 participants (1,593 survey, 653 market), about 177 per condition, 7% attrition.
quote: Remarkably, a brief probabilistic training module paid off over an extended time
limits: Sample needed a bachelor's degree. Scores standardized within question. See GJP subfield 02 for team and tracking numbers.
agent_relevance: Probability training (reference class, averaging, avoid overconfidence and base-rate neglect) was the better module. Scenario training was weaker, so do not invest in scenario generation for single forecasts.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament (Psychological Science)
finding: Training improved both calibration and resolution. Overconfidence was worse without training in both years.
numbers: Calibration: Y1 F(2,1586)=3.16, p=.04; Y2 F(1,938)=3.78, p<.05. Resolution: Y1 F(2,1586)=18.50, p<.001; Y2 F(1,871)=16.23, p<.001. All calibration-curve points fell below the identity line (overconfidence), worst without training. Calibration worst at forecasts of 100% from lack of updating.
limits: Training effect is smaller than the effect of teaming (Y1 F=60.68) and tracking.
agent_relevance: Training ranks below teaming and tracking in size, so for the agent it is one lever of three and the cheapest.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament (Psychological Science)
finding: Training and teaming effects were not just because trained people forecast later or updated more. The regression check kept the effects significant when timing and update count were added.
numbers: Regressions with dummy variables for training and teaming plus timing of first forecast and number of updates; effects stayed significant (as stated in text). Table 1 gives Brier by first week, middle 2 weeks and last week.
limits: Coefficients not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Suggests training changes judgement quality, not only effort.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament (Psychological Science)
finding: Training module design: interactive, with questions and answers to check understanding. Probability training told people to use reference classes, average estimates from models, polls and expert panels, extrapolate time series, and avoid overconfidence, confirmation bias and base-rate neglect. Scenario training taught generating new futures, decision trees, and avoiding probabilities that sum above 1.
numbers: Design drew on O'Hagan et al. 2006 elicitation advice. Earlier candidate methods listed: statistical training (Fong et al. 1986), feedback (Benson & Onkal 1992), multiple perspectives, historical analogies (Lovallo et al. 2012), decomposition, contrary evidence (Koriat et al. 1980).
limits: Exact slides not in the paper.
agent_relevance: Gives the concrete list of moves to copy into prompt steps.

source: Lichtenstein & Fischhoff (1980) Training for calibration (Organizational Behavior and Human Performance 26)
finding: Founding calibration training study: people given feedback on many general-knowledge items became better calibrated. As described by Moore 2017: 45 minutes of training followed by 22 hour-long test sessions.
numbers: 45 min training plus 22 sessions of 1 hour (as reported by Moore et al. 2017). Exact calibration scores not read.
limits: Not opened; gains reported to degrade and transfer weakly. General-knowledge items, not forecasts.
agent_relevance: Calibration feedback on many items helps, and the gain fades.

source: Stone & Opel (2000) Training to improve calibration and discrimination (Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes)
finding: Training study on calibration vs discrimination, as summarized by Moore et al.: 6 test sessions of 2 hours each, some benefit for overconfidence.
numbers: 6 sessions x 2 hours (as reported by Moore et al. 2017). Effect sizes not read.
limits: Not opened; I did not verify any calibration versus discrimination trade-off in the original.
agent_relevance: Check both calibration and discrimination when we score the agent.

source: Fong, Krantz, Nisbett (1986) The effects of statistical training on thinking about everyday problems (Cognitive Psychology)
finding: Short statistical training raised use of statistical reasoning in everyday problems. Cited by Mellers 2014 as a basis for statistical-training claims.
numbers: Not read; numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule-based statistical reminder over an abstract bias warning.

source: Larrick, Morgan, Nisbett (1990) Teaching the use of cost-benefit reasoning in everyday life (Psychological Science)
finding: Training in cost-benefit principles improved everyday decisions for both educated and uneducated people. Cited in Chang 2016 as process-based debiasing.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Process training can transfer outside the training domain in humans.

source: Lehman & Nisbett (1990) A longitudinal study of the effects of undergraduate training on reasoning (Developmental Psychology)
finding: Statistical training in undergraduate majors improved probabilistic reasoning. Chang 2016 reports a weak link between SAT scores and the gain.
numbers: r = 0.16, p < .06 between SAT and reasoning gain, as reported in Chang et al. 2016.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Gain from training is only weakly tied to ability in this study.

source: Sedlmeier & Gigerenzer (2001) Teaching Bayesian reasoning in less than two hours (J. Experimental Psychology: General)
finding: Teaching people to turn probability problems into natural frequencies raised Bayesian reasoning quickly. Cited by Chang 2016.
numbers: Not read; numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Frequency format is a cheap prompt device for base-rate arithmetic; not tested in LLMs here.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities
finding: Preregistered test of 38 prompts (control plus 37) on 100 ForecastBench questions with four non-reasoning LLMs. The main model found no prompt that improved Brier score robustly by the strict test. Base-rate and frequency prompts were the best: small gains.
numbers: Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B, temp 0. About 3,636 to 3,771 usable forecasts per model. Control mean Brier per model about 0.21 (GPT-4o 0.215, Haiku 0.214). One-sample t-tests, mean Brier difference from control: Frequency-Based Reasoning -0.019 (SD 0.114, n=370, p=.001, adj p=.022); Base Rate First -0.016 (SD 0.106, n=390, p=.003, adj p=.036). Step-Back also better after BH correction.
quote: references to base rates yield slight benefits
limits: Gains of 0.016 to 0.019 on a base near 0.21 are under 10%. In the stricter preregistered mixed model no prompt was significantly better. Only 100 questions.
agent_relevance: The LLM version of the outside-view lesson gives about 0.02 Brier. That is the size to expect, not a big jump.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities
finding: Asking the model to reason in Bayesian terms (start with a prior, update) made forecasts worse in all models, as did a propose-evaluate-select prompt. Those two effects survived multiple-comparison correction.
numbers: Bayesian Reasoning: mean Brier difference +0.025 (SD 0.172, n=388, p=.005, adj p=.036); mixed-model coefficient about +0.03, p<.001. Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.028 (SD 0.153, n=391, p<.001, adj p=.010). These prompts and Chain of Thought made forecasts more decisive: 17.2 to 19.9 points from 50%, vs 11.9 to 13.4 for control, Re-Reading and anchoring warning.
limits: Authors' explanation (superficial mimicry of Bayesian updating) is a guess, not tested.
agent_relevance: Direct warning against telling the agent to do explicit Bayes in text. Teach the reference class, not Bayes arithmetic. Matches G1: forced extra deliberation can hurt.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities
finding: Study 2 tested compound prompts and prompts from outside sources (Anthropic and OpenAI auto-prompts, superforecaster-authored, scratchpad from Halawi 2024) on six models including o1 and o1-mini. Prompt engineering made negligible difference overall.
numbers: About 19,000 forecasts targeted per model. Mean Brier: o1-mini 0.217, o1 0.216, Llama 3.1 405B 0.218, GPT-4o 0.208, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.207. Mean forecast 41.5% (o1) to 44.8% (Llama); Base Rate First plus Frequency-Based combo had mean forecast 38.4%.
quote: the effect of prompting on forecasting accuracy is negligible
limits: Reasoning models did not beat non-reasoning models here. Questions mostly from ForecastBench.
agent_relevance: Stacking more training-like text does not add up. A better base model matters more than a better prompt.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: A retrieval-augmented GPT-4 system with an optimized scratchpad prompt and a model fine-tuned on its own best forecasts came close to the human crowd. The scratchpad asks the model to rephrase the question, list arguments, weigh them, and check base rate and over- or under-confidence.
numbers: Test set: questions after June 2023, five platforms. System Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149; best baseline model 0.208; ablation with no fine-tuning and no retrieval 0.206; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 version 0.182. Weighted average with crowd (4x crowd weight) 0.146. Accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%. Fine-tuning data: 73,632 generated reasonings, 13,253 kept, 6,000 used for 2 epochs. Calibration RMS error 0.42 vs crowd 0.38.
limits: Crowd still better overall; system near crowd on Sports, far behind on Environment. Gains split between retrieval and fine-tuning, not isolated to the base-rate prompt step.
agent_relevance: Closest analogue of training for LLMs: fine-tune on forecasts that beat the crowd. Not available to a scaffold-only plan, but the scratchpad step list including a base-rate check is.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR)
finding: Superforecasters beat the best LLM on a 200-question subset. The best LLMs had access to the crowd forecast on market questions.
numbers: Brier: superforecasters 0.096, general public 0.121, top LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122, best LLM without crowd value 0.136. 39 superforecasters in a 9-day experiment. LLMs significantly worse on combination questions.
limits: Human medians compared to single-model forecasts; 200 of 1,000 questions had human forecasts.
agent_relevance: Measured gap between trained experts and LLMs that training-style scaffolds aim to narrow.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on real-world forecasting against expert forecasters
finding: On 464 Metaculus questions, frontier LLMs now beat the crowd baseline but are well behind the expert group. Prompt told the model it was a superforecaster and to think of factors that move the forecast up or down.
numbers: o3 Brier 0.1352 vs crowd baseline 0.149 (Halawi) and 0.121 (Karger); paper reports experts 0.023 vs o3 0.135. o3-pro on a hold-out set 0.1307. Five samples per question, mean and median reported. Models typically overconfident, especially on events they rate likely. Direct prompt did better than narrative prompt.
limits: Brier not comparable across question sets; the 0.023 expert figure looks like a selected set and is hard to interpret. Paper originally called the experts superforecasters (trademark note).
agent_relevance: A persona prompt plus a request for a range is the common cheap baseline. Overconfidence at high stated probabilities persists in newer models.

source: Schoenegger & Park (2023) Large language model prediction capabilities: evidence from a real-world forecasting tournament
finding: GPT-4 entered a Metaculus tournament with a prompt built on forecasting research (superforecaster persona, use base rates, long rationale). It did not beat a no-information baseline and lost to the crowd.
numbers: GPT-4 mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.18) vs human crowd 0.07 (SD 0.08); difference 0.13, t(44)=3.11, p=.003, d=0.94. GPT-4 not significantly better than the 0.25 baseline. 843 participants, July to October 2023, binary questions.
limits: Single chat window, small question set, early model.
agent_relevance: A forecasting-lesson prompt alone did not help an early model. The lesson needs a capable base model and retrieval.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd (Science Advances)
finding: A crowd of twelve LLMs matched a crowd of 925 humans on 31 binary questions. Giving the models the human median improved their accuracy.
numbers: Study 1: LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=.850. Study 2: exposure to median human forecast improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 accuracy by 17% to 28%. Acquiescence: mean predictions above 50% despite near-even outcomes. Prompt uses superforecaster persona.
limits: Only 31 questions; equivalence was exploratory.
agent_relevance: An outside anchor (crowd median) works in LLMs. The analog for our agent is a computed base rate from a reference class.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Skotheim, Hewitt, Schoenegger (2025) Outcome-based reinforcement learning to predict the future (TMLR)
finding: RL on resolved Polymarket outcomes with a Brier-based reward made a 14B reasoning model match o1 on accuracy and improve calibration. This is training on forecasts, in weights.
numbers: 1,265 held-out questions. Soft-Brier / ECE: DeepSeek-R1 14B base 0.215 / 0.089; ReMax ensemble-7 0.190 [0.178, 0.203] / 0.062; modified GRPO 0.192 / 0.054; o1 0.202 / 0.093; Polymarket price 0.151 / 0.043. Brier diff vs base -0.025 (p<.001). Simulated one-share trades: $52 vs o1 $39.
limits: Market price still better than every model. Uses news headlines up to prediction date; leakage guards but not zero risk.
agent_relevance: Weight training works and shows the same calibration-first benefit as human training, but it is outside our scaffold-only scope.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and tools for human-level forecasting
finding: ReAct agents with tools beat chain-of-thought and scratchpad prompting with fine-tuning and matched human median forecasts on Brier. Ensembles helped only when each member was already calibrated.
numbers: RTF Brier 0.169 vs human median 0.172; accuracy 73.9% vs 73.8%. Ensemble RTF 0.169 vs single 0.180. Base GPT-4o ensemble 0.218 vs single 0.210 (ensemble worse). Halawi et al. GPT-4o listed 0.177.
limits: Only the results text and table were read, not the full method.
agent_relevance: Matches G4: averaging samples from poorly calibrated models does not help.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: LLMs show bias patterns like humans (framing, anchoring, group attribution, primacy). Zero-shot warnings (awareness) gave small improvements. Few-shot debiasing often failed and pushed outputs to extremes.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under reject framing; Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Self-help (model rewrites its own prompt) did better than awareness for primacy bias on Llama-2 and GPT-4.
limits: Admissions task, not forecasting. No calibration outcome.
agent_relevance: A plain 'be aware of bias' line barely helps LLMs, matching the human finding that didactic debiasing is weak.
